source.title: GShard: Scaling Giant Models with Conditional Computation and Automatic Sharding
source.authors: Dmitry Lepikhin; HyoukJoong Lee; Yuan-Zhong Xu; Dehao Chen; O. Firat; Yan-Ping Huang; M. Krikun; Noam Shazeer; Z. Chen

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses model scaling to build and evaluate multilingual machine-translation models, but does not test the language-model loss laws or compute-optimal allocation described in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work for power-law scaling, but reports its own multilingual machine-translation results, not held-out language-model pretraining loss, fits of scaling laws, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its reported translation-quality and training-loss results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: GShard is a systems paper. It cites Kaplan et al. for power-law scaling but fits no power law, reports no held-out LM pretraining loss, and does not examine compute-optimal allocation or extrapolation. Its results are BLEU and training cross-entropy for six MoE translation models at a single 1T-token budget. These show quality rising with size but do not test the power-law form in any version. It does not rely on the scaling law as a tool either, so it is cites_only rather than T4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' main conclusion is that GShard lets a 600B-parameter sparse MoE MT model train in 4 days on 2048 TPUs (22 TPU core-years versus 29 for 100 bilingual baselines) with far better quality. They also say quality gains have not plateaued, and that capacity bottleneck, positive transfer and parameter counting complicate comparisons across model sizes.
record.recipe_differences: This is a multilingual machine-translation scaling study using sparsely gated MoE Transformers and GShard, not a language-model held-out-loss scaling-law fit.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported translation quality and training efficiency vary with expert count and depth; the authors also describe capacity bottlenecks and differing high- versus low-resource outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Multilingual MoE MT models report average BLEU above bilingual baselines. BLEU is not ordered by parameter count: 150B (43.7) beats 200B (41.3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In multilingual MoE MT, translation quality rises with model capacity, but depth and expert count matter beyond raw parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed 12L depth, going from 128 to 512 experts gave +3.3 BLEU, and from 512 to 2048 only +1.3 BLEU. The authors call this diminishing returns.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert-count scaling in MoE MT shows diminishing BLEU returns past a capacity bottleneck.

fits_no_version.finding: Deeper MoE models (36L vs 12L) needed 2–3x fewer tokens to reach a training cross-entropy threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE MT, deeper models are more sample-efficient on training loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Authors state that parameter counting does not always correlate with effective capacity at scale. This is a qualitative argument, not a fitted law.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For sparse MoE models, total parameter count is a poor proxy for effective capacity.

record.problems: The reported loss measurements are training cross-entropy for multilingual machine translation, not held-out language-model pretraining loss. The paper does not fit or evaluate power laws or compute-optimal allocations for the claim.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately reported results bearing on the claim were left out.

untested.parts: No held-out LM pretraining loss and no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. All runs use a fixed 1T-token budget.
Depth (12L vs 36L) changes both parameter count and BLEU, so this is not a fixed-parameter shape comparison.
MT is a different regime, but no power-law form is fitted to its loss or BLEU.
BLEU is the task metric of the trained MT model, not a downstream task of a pretrained LM. It is not related to scale by any predictive fit.
No fitted exponents or allocations are compared.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T4/uses_without_test should be cites_only/T6: the paper cites the power-law finding as motivation but does not use it as a tool. All loss values are training cross-entropy excluding the auxiliary loss, not held-out loss. The MoE models share one token budget (1T), so there is no data or compute axis to fit.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss of language models and power-law relationships with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation from small language-model runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as compute grows.
Architecture comparisons at a fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss; the reported task is multilingual machine translation, not a downstream evaluation of a pretrained language model.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.
